concept.name: Underwater curve
concept.definition: The time series of percentage (or absolute) drawdown from the running equity peak, plotted as a persistently non-positive curve that touches zero only at new equity highs. It is the drawdown view of the equity curve, showing the depth and duration of every loss episode at a glance.
concept.intuition: Flip the equity curve's perspective: instead of how high you've climbed, the underwater curve shows how far below the surface you've spent your time.
concept.mechanics: At each period compute (running peak - current equity) / running peak and plot it; the depth (maximum drawdown), width (time under water / drawdown duration), and area of the resulting episodes summarize the strategy's pain profile better than the equity curve alone.
concept.formula: UW_t = ( E_t - max_{s<=t} E_s ) / max_{s<=t} E_s <= 0, where E_t is equity at time t.
concept.failure_modes: It inherits every flaw of drawdown statistics: sample dependence, censoring of unrecovered episodes, and flattering by smoothed marks; and it hides the return side — two strategies with identical underwater curves can have very different compound returns.
concept.misconceptions: A brief, shallow underwater curve does not prove a safe strategy — it may simply never have met a regime shift — and a curve not back at zero by the sample end means the worst episode is still running, not that it ended.
concept.example: A fund whose equity peaked 14 months ago and sits 8% below that peak shows an underwater curve pinned at -8% for the whole episode, making the recovery burden (an 8.7% gain is needed) explicit.
